headline_summary: Home sales at 16-year low; VIX elevated
month_in_brief: Unemployment is low at 4.1%; mortgage rates near 7.3% coincide with the slowest home sales since 2010 and supply of 5.1 months. Builder confidence, flipping returns and permits are down, nationally and in Texas. Apartment rents are flat nationally and lower in Texas metros. Office and industrial vacancy are off their peaks. Household credit is split: card stress is easing, auto and overall delinquency are rising, and foreclosures are up from low levels.
big_picture: Jobs are still solid by historical standards, but borrowing costs are high and existing-home sales are at a 16-year low. Builders are pulling back on new permits, especially in Texas. Household credit is split: credit card losses are easing, while auto and overall delinquency, bankruptcies and foreclosures are rising from low levels.

notes.comparisons: Arrows show direction vs. a year ago (▲ ▼ ▶). Color shows how the change is generally read: green favorable, red unfavorable, black flat or mixed (e.g., higher prices help owners but hurt buyers). Data only; no forecast. *Oct 2025 unemployment not collected (shutdown); Sep 2025 used.
notes.key_indicators: Arrows compare the latest reading with the same period one year earlier (y/y); the '2019' column is a separate pre-pandemic reference and is not used for the arrow. Color: green = generally read as favorable for the broad economy, red = generally read as unfavorable, black = flat or mixed. *October 2025 unemployment was not collected (government shutdown). Bankruptcies 2025–26 from Epiq; 2019 from U.S. Courts. Texas permits are not seasonally adjusted.
notes.correlations: Correlation runs from −1 to +1; it shows that two series moved together, not that one caused the other. Only 20 annual data points; the card charge-off figure excludes 2020–21 pandemic years. The next-year relationship uses 18 pairs of years.
notes.inventory: Land and commercial turn over far more slowly than homes, so compare them with their own history. Statewide land months of inventory is not published. Medians shift with the mix of properties sold, and land and commercial rest on small samples.
notes.tx_metros: Sources: Census building permits via FRED (metro, not seasonally adjusted); Apartment List Rent Index; Yardi Matrix office vacancy.
notes.vix_rule: The banner uses the latest VIX close. Below 20: normal. 20–29.99: elevated, the level commonly watched as a sign of heightened uncertainty. 30–39.99: high alert, a level historically associated with market stress. 40 and above: extreme, historically seen only in acute crises (2008, 2020). A separate flag appears when the 10-yr minus 2-yr Treasury spread is below zero (inverted).
notes.c1_caption: Annual averages. Sources: BLS via FRED (UNRATE); Freddie Mac PMMS via FRED (MORTGAGE30US). Shaded: 2008–09 recession, 2020 pandemic.
notes.c2_caption: Sources: RealtyTrac/ATTOM year-end reports (2014, 2021 and 2024 derived from reported % changes); U.S. Courts (2007–08 are fiscal years).
notes.c6_caption: Fitch restated the index in July 2026; earlier bars are pre-restatement and not directly comparable.
notes.c8_caption: MHI shipments 2006–2024; MHARR production 2025. The two series are not identical.
notes.c17_caption: Annual averages, 2006 to 2026 YTD. The 20-year dollar panel uses the Fed broad trade-weighted index (26 currencies), which differs from the six-currency DXY.

bullets.text: Mortgage rates (7.28%) are well above the 20-year average (4.8%); existing sales are at the slowest pace since 2010.
Prices are flat nationally (+0.4%) and slightly lower in Texas (statewide median down about 3% in October).
Texas listings rose 2.8% in Q3, giving buyers more choice.
Builder confidence 25, the lowest since April 2012; 46% of builders cut prices in November.
U.S. permits in 2025 were 18% below the 2021 high (October pace 25% below); Texas 2025 was 20% below its 2022 peak; Houston and Austin about −14% this year.
Texas metros are still working through a large apartment supply wave, so rents are falling now.

themes.title: Jobs: steady, softer at the edges

bullets.text: Unemployment 4.1% and weekly claims 203,000 are low by 20-year standards.
Average job search is 27.1 weeks, recent-graduate unemployment is 5.6%, and AI-cited layoffs rose in 2026 before falling to 1,265 in October.
total announced layoffs are down 44% (Jan–Oct vs. Jan–Oct 2025).
card charge-offs (3.82%) are below a year ago; new card serious delinquencies are at the lowest since Q1 2024.
total delinquency 4.96%, highest since 2016; new auto 90+ day delinquencies highest since 2010; bankruptcies up each year since 2022; foreclosure filings +21% (H1).
foreclosures are about one-eighth of the 2010 peak.

c1_bullets.text: Mortgage rates bottomed at a 2.96% annual average (2021); 2023–2025 (6.6–6.8%) are slightly above 2006–07 levels (6.3–6.4%).

c2_bullets.text: Foreclosures peaked at 2.87M properties (2010); 2025 was 367,460, about one-eighth of the peak.
Bankruptcies peaked at 1.59M (2010); 2025 was 574,314, up each year since the 2022 low; foreclosures rose 14% in 2025.

bullets.text: AI-cited cuts 12,742 in 2024 and 54,836 in 2025; 2026 peaked at 38,579 in May and was 1,265 in October.
AI was the top stated reason every month from March to July 2026, then below 10% of monthly cuts in August–October.
Unemployment 4.1% (Oct) with 165,000 jobs added, vs. a prior 12-month average of 48,000; recent-graduate unemployment 5.6% (Q2, NY Fed); average job search 27.1 weeks.
Card charge-offs 3.82% (Q2 2026) vs. 4.19% a year earlier: near 2019 (3.78%), well below the 2009 peak (10.54%).
Seriously late (90+ days): student loans 10.9%, autos 5.66%, the highest since the series began in 2003.
4.96% of all household debt is in some stage of delinquency, up from 4.48% a year ago, the highest since 2016; card balances 90+ days late 12.9% (2010 peak 13.74%).
Inflation 3.7% (Sep) is energy-led: energy +20.4% y/y, while core is 2.6%. No October annual rate was published (2025 shutdown); October rose 0.4% on the month.

bullets.text: Futures implied a >90% chance of a 0.25-pt hike at the Dec 8–9 meeting (as of Nov 17).
Big Tech 2026 plans: Amazon ~$220B, Alphabet $195–205B, Meta $135–145B (~$245B total in 2024).
S&P 500 hit its lowest close since late July on Nov 17; junk-bond spread 3.52 pts, below the ~5 pts seen in past stress periods.
Yield curve +0.30 pts on Nov 17, not inverted; 2026 low of 0.22 pts. It was inverted for most of 2022–2024; inversions have preceded past recessions.
VIX closed at 24.52 on Nov 18, after spiking 70% to 28.18 on Nov 5; 2026 average 18.2 vs. 32.7 in 2008 and 29.3 in 2020.
Dollar index reached a 19-month high of 103.97 on Nov 19; +3.5% y/y; much of the rise reflects a weaker euro; the Fed broad index rose ~2% in 2026 through Nov 6.

permit_bullets.text: U.S. permits at a 1.295M annual pace in October, the lowest since May 2020; single-family 772,000, down 12.9%.
Texas 147,854 units Jan–Sep 2026, 9.6% below the same months of 2025; the state peaked at 261,230 in 2022 vs. 82,104 in 2009.
U.S. 2025 total 1.43M, below the 2021 high (1.74M) and above the 2009 low (583,000).

sales_bullets.text: Existing home sales 3.75M pace (Oct), lowest since 2010; pending-sales index 63.0, a record low; median price $416,700 (+0.4% y/y).
Mortgage delinquency 4.42%, +0.43 pts vs. a year ago (Q3, MBA); FHA foreclosure rate 1.89%, highest since 2017.

mh_bullets.text: Shipments ~103,000 in 2025, double the 2009–10 low; 2026 production −5.1% Jan–Aug (MHARR); average new price $129,400 (Jun 2026) vs. $84,400 (Jun 2019).

inventory.how_to_read: Months of inventory = listings for sale ÷ sales per month. A higher number means more choice for buyers and more competition among sellers; a lower number means the reverse. Benchmarks differ: NAHB cites 4.5–6 months as balanced nationally; Texas sources have cited 3–4 months (Texas Real Estate Research Center) or 4–5 months (Texas Realtors).

bullets.text: U.S. supply 5.1 months, the highest since November 2015, as sales fell to a 16-year low.
Houston supply at a 14-year high (5.5 vs. 5.1 months a year ago); Dallas–FW has the least supply of the four big metros at 4.6 months.
Austin and San Antonio are roughly unchanged from a year ago, near 5.5–6 months.

Moody's measure rose from 16.8% (2019) to a record 20.7% (2025). Other firms measure differently but show the same direction now: CBRE 18.2% (−0.6 pts y/y), Yardi 17.8% (−0.8 pts y/y). CBRE prime space 11.9%; completions −76% y/y. Badge-ins ~56% of 2019.
vacancy 6.8% (C&W), down from a 7.0% peak in late 2025 and the lowest since end-2024; deliveries −13% YTD, but space under construction +23% y/y.
among the tightest sectors at 4.3% (Colliers); shopping centers 5.9% vs. ~7% pre-pandemic; malls 8.2%.

Houston office 25.6% by Newmark's measure (23.6% Yardi), flat; leasing at its weakest since 2009.
DFW industrial 7.8% (CBRE), down from 8.9% a year ago; DFW leads the U.S. in industrial space under construction.

bullets.text: Houston (−14.3%) and Austin (−14.7%) fell the most; San Antonio rose 4.3% from a low 2025 base; Austin's 2025 total was 45% below its 2021 peak.
all four metros are below a year ago while the U.S. is +0.1%; San Antonio has the steepest decline of any large U.S. metro; about 32% of properties nationally advertise a month or more free.
